It was another successful year of Performances in the Park despite attendance being down, according to the Central Cariboo Arts and Culture Society. At a Nov. 25 Central Cariboo Joint Committee meeting, executive director Melissa Normandin provided an overview of the free, family-friendly summer concert series that brought live music and cultural performances in Boitanio Park for Williams Lake residents and visitors from July 9 to Aug. 27. An average of 219 attendees were welcomed each evening, marking a small decrease from the 2025 season that had an average weekly attendance of 237. “Attendance was a bit down and I’m going to blame the weather for that,” Normandin said. Of the 16 different performers or acts participating in this year’s Performances in the Park seven were local. A total program budget of $36,155 supported through diversified funding sources including local government, community sponsorships and in-kind contributions. In June, Williams Lake First Nation was added as a core funding partner with the City of Williams Lake and Cariboo Regional District for a three year term that includes an annual payment of $22,000 to the society for eight summer events. Normandin said their budget dollars were pretty consistent with previous years, and if they had more they could probably review some different asks received from the community including shade and covered areas. Cleanliness and adequately supplied washroom facilities throughout the evening was another challenge, along with glass, and broken bottles and garbage. “We can tackle that, and hopefully work with the city on that,” Normandin said. Mayor Surinderpal Rathor said he attended every concert and encouraged organizers to keep up the good work. On Monday, Nov. 23, Del Rosario was joined by Nystoruk at Save-On-Foods where he held his first Pick a Square Fundraiser that pulled in $714. A preliminary assessment of the post-wildfire hazards of the Pear Lake wildfire near Clinton this past summer show that homes, highways, and infrastructure such as the CN rail line and a BC Hydro substation are at elevated risk from flooding, debris flows, and landslides in the fire’s aftermath. The Pear Lake wildfire was reported on July 17, and was not declared under control until Sept. 14. It burned a total area of 165,909 hectares (1,659 square kilometres), forced the evacuation of thousands of residents, and destroyed more than 120 structures, including homes. The report — dated Oct. 8 and released on Nov. 9 — is largely based on aerial reconnaissance carried out in August. The report’s author, geomorphologist Sarah Crookshanks, notes that it was prepared on an expedited basis so that a Level 4 Detailed Assessment can be started. The fire affected 28 watersheds, with some seeing up to 99 per cent of their area burned. The Clinton Creek watershed (6,663 hectares) saw 86 per cent of its area burned, with 76 per cent of that burned at moderate or high severity. Some 50 per cent of the Big Bar Creek watershed (45,156 hectares in total) was burned, and 41 per cent of the Maiden Creek watershed (5,955 hectares) was burned. The report states that potential elements at risk include residential structures on private properties; First Nations lands; the Highway 97 and Highway 99 corridors; secondary public roads, including the Clinton-Pavilion Road and the southern part of Jesmond Road; provincial parks at Marble Range, Big Bar Lake, Downing, and Chasm; the CN rail mainline; the BC Hydro transmission line and substation near Kelly Lake; and water resources and infrastructure in the Clinton Community Watershed.

Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. The release of water from the Cheakamus Dam flooded roads near Squamish and was intended to make room in the reservoir for more rain. Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. Rain eased in some areas, but Vancouver Island remained under rainfall and flood warnings, and forecasters were tracking more storm systems expected over the weekend.

items.content_html:

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

Springfield, Massachusetts, has not advanced a proposed ban; councilors plan to review possible safeguards before deciding whether to send it forward. The systems record plates, timestamps and locations. Police say they can help investigate crimes and find missing people, while privacy advocates warn about tracking, misuse and data sharing beyond local jurisdictions. Suffolk County’s sheriff’s office has data-sharing relationships with slightly more than 400 agencies, established through system settings rather than formal written agreements. Ohio lawmakers are considering House Bill 725, which would set statewide rules for police use of plate data and make misuse a fifth-degree felony. The ACLU of Ohio argues the bill regulates data only after collection and could reduce public access to search information. Springfield’s committee plans to meet again after consulting the city’s Law Department.

items.title: [nacion.com] Latin American countries raise the alarm over rising diabetes rates and underdiagnosis
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Health figures released for World Diabetes Day show diagnoses and undetected cases in several Latin American countries. Costa Rica reported 17,276 diagnoses in 2025, 28.62% more than in 2024; in Panama, the Social Security Fund treated around 53,000 people during 2025, while an estimated 312,800 adults were living with diabetes in 2024. In Mexico, more than 14 million adults have the disease, and nearly one in three is unaware of their diagnosis. National estimates do not necessarily use the same methods. In Brazil, an estimated five million people remain undiagnosed, in addition to the 16 million who have been diagnosed. In Argentina, nearly four in 10 people with abnormal test results were unaware of their condition. The International Diabetes Federation estimates that more than 589 million adults worldwide are living with diabetes. Type 2 diabetes can progress for years without clear symptoms; when blood glucose remains high, it can cause cardiovascular, kidney, vision, and nerve damage. Authorities and specialists recommend screening tests, clinical follow-up, and sustained lifestyle changes. Costa Rica recorded another 16,758 new cases up to the epidemiological week of October 18–24, 2026.

items.title: [agri-mutuel.com] French institute plans AI farm adviser as Deere expands data tool
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

France’s public agricultural research institute INRAE plans to build an AI assistant using verified scientific data to help farmers respond to climate change and other pressures. The project awaits approval for €1.2 million in France 2030 funding, with a first version planned for farmer testing within 18 months. Separately, John Deere expanded access to its free JD assistant on Nov. 16, linking it to the company’s Operations Center farm-management platform. INRAE’s proposed assistant would tailor guidance to a farm’s location, practices, soil, expected water resources and finances, while Deere’s tool searches and analyzes information already recorded about a user’s fields, machinery and farm operations. INRAE says the project has demonstrated answers to simple queries and aims to handle more complex questions; farmer testing depends on the funding decision.

items.title: [cnbc.com] France-led protests spread to 31 European countries as rallies continue
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

France’s protest movement over living costs, wages and public services has spread to 30 other European countries, with more than 1,700 demonstrations recorded across the continent from Sept. 15 to Oct. 30, according to an analysis of Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) figures. In France, the protests began with students challenging school conditions and widened to include unions and other groups. On Saturday, Nov. 7, the Interior Ministry counted 146,000 demonstrators nationwide, including 46,000 in Paris; unions estimated 250,000 and 75,000, respectively. It was the fourth consecutive Saturday of protests, and clashes followed in Paris and other cities. French authorities deployed about 70,000 security personnel on Saturday. The Interior Ministry recorded at least 360 arrests nationwide, according to AFP. Attendance was down from earlier weekends and from Thursday’s union rally, which drew 575,000 people by the government’s count. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to meet labor unions and employer representatives on Monday, Nov. 9, to discuss wages and purchasing power. Student and teacher groups have called for a strike on Tuesday, while France’s Senate is scheduled to begin debating the government’s 2027 budget proposal on Nov. 20.

items.title: [abcnews.com] Trump replaces national cyber director after outages disrupt US services
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

President Donald Trump replaced National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross with Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies as acting director after a week of outages disrupted aviation, banking, communications and government systems. The incidents have drawn scrutiny of the administration’s response, although officials say there is no evidence of a coordinated cyberattack or a connection among the failures. A source familiar with the White House’s thinking said Trump supported Cairncross’s removal because he lacked strong cybersecurity credentials. Trump said Friday, “I didn’t think that person was good enough”. Axios reported that Chief of Staff Stephen Miller pushed for the change on similar grounds. Cairncross, a former Republican National Committee executive, said he was proud of his work in the role. Davies has held cybersecurity and technology leadership jobs at Unilever, Estée Lauder, Barclays-Africa Group, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Siemens. Davies will serve temporarily. A permanent director must be nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, which Democrats are due to control in January. Cybersecurity experts say companies’ rapid efforts to patch software vulnerabilities may be behind some disruptions, as advanced AI tools make those flaws easier to find.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] Leo XIV warns of rural exodus at Mass in the Peruvian Andes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Pope Leo XIV warned on Saturday during a Mass in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, in the Peruvian Andes, that poverty, forced migration, and the unequal distribution of resources are emptying rural communities. Around 20,000 people attended, according to the Vatican. Leo XIV, who led the Diocese of Chiclayo, thus fulfilled his promise to return to Peru, made before leaving for Rome in 2023. In his homily, he spoke of those who leave their towns to seek a better future in coastal cities and urged people to confront injustice without violence. Cajamarca, the region where Santa Cruz is located, has poverty rates of up to 40%, according to official figures cited by Reuters. On Saturday, Leo XIV also crowned the image of the Immaculate Conception at Chiclayo Cathedral and closed the jubilee year in Zaña, marking the 300th anniversary of the canonization of Saint Toribio de Mogrovejo. This Sunday, November 15, he travels to Cusco and Pucallpa, where he will meet with missionaries and representatives of Amazonian peoples; on Monday, November 16, he will celebrate the concluding Mass in Lima before departing for Rome.

items.title: [space.com] Researchers grow potatoes in simulated lunar soil using 30% compost
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Oregon State University researchers grew potatoes through their full life cycle in simulated lunar regolith after adding organic matter; a mixture containing 30% vermicompost produced yields comparable to those in terrestrial soil. The NASA-funded experiment took place in a greenhouse on Earth and used simulated material, not material collected on the moon, so it does not establish that crops can be grown on the lunar surface. The trial used five regolith simulants and the Modoc potato variety. Researchers plan to test 10 more potato varieties and are studying growth in larger pots; the first trial’s small pots produced small tubers.

items.title: [scmp.com] Trump threatens tax on U.S. tech firms building AI data centres abroad
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

President Donald Trump threatened a “tremendous tax” on U.S. technology companies that build artificial-intelligence data centres overseas, saying the facilities should remain in the United States to prevent China from gaining access to computing capacity. He gave no details on the proposed penalty and said he had not discussed it with his administration, leaving unclear how it could be imposed. Trump urged communities to accept domestic projects and negotiate payments or other benefits from developers. About three-quarters of U.S. voters opposed building a data centre in their community, with residents citing electricity prices and water use as concerns. The administration is tightening restrictions on remote access to advanced U.S. chips and servers to prevent Chinese firms from using computing capacity hosted in third countries. Technology companies are offering communities more transparency, environmental commitments and financial contributions to secure approval for projects.

🏔️ ✏️

The Council of the European Union and the European Parliament reached a provisional agreement on Nov. 18 to speed up permitting for renewable energy projects, electricity grids and storage facilities, aiming to reduce construction delays and strengthen energy security. The changes also cover recharging stations and authorizations for new electricity and gas infrastructure. The agreement streamlines deadlines for approvals and grid connections and provides for digital portals to handle applications. Both institutions must still endorse and formally adopt it after a legal and linguistic review; member states will then have 18 months to incorporate the directive into national law.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Breathing less oxygen tripled lifespan in mice with a deadly brain disorder
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Oxygen is essential for life, but too much of it can become dangerously toxic, particularly in people with certain neurological and mitochondrial disorders. Scientists at Gladstone Institutes have discovered that defective proteins can disrupt the ability of mitochondria to consume oxygen, allowing harmful levels to accumulate in tissues. Remarkably, mice with a genetic disorder that causes motor neuron degeneration lived three times longer when they breathed air containing less oxygen.

items.title: [simon42.com] Home Assistant Beta enables camera recordings with HomeKit Secure Video in Apple Home
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The second beta of the smart home software Home Assistant 2026.12 makes it possible for the first time to connect cameras via the HomeKit Bridge and save their recordings with HomeKit Secure Video in Apple Home. Until now, the Bridge only transmitted live video; additional software was needed for recordings. Requirements include an Apple home hub, an iCloud+ subscription, a motion sensor, and setting up the camera as a standalone HomeKit accessory. Recording must be enabled separately for each camera. Recordings only start when motion is detected. As a result, the first few seconds may be missing. Home Assistant recommends H.264 streams, since conversion via FFmpeg uses processing power. In the developer test, an H.265 source failed to meet the Apple home hub’s time limit. The final version is planned for December 2, 2026; until then, beta features may still change.

items.title: [elpais.com] Leo XIV denounces racism against Afro-Peruvians and recalls slavery
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Pope Leo XIV denounced the discrimination that Afro-Peruvians continue to face on November 14 and recalled the slavery and humiliation suffered by their ancestors. He did so during a meeting in Zaña, a town in northern Peru recognized as a site commemorating slavery and African cultural heritage. Leo expressed his affection for the community and spoke about crime, extortion, and insecurity affecting families in the area. The pontiff, who was bishop of the Diocese of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, closed in Zaña the Jubilee Year marking the 300th anniversary of the canonization of Saint Toribio de Mogrovejo. In May, in his first encyclical, he had apologized on behalf of the Church for the role previous pontiffs played in legitimizing slavery in the Americas and for failing to condemn it for centuries. At the meeting, Analí Montenegro Mendoza, representative of the Afro-Peruvian community in the diocese, called for a Church in which no one feels inferior because of their skin color, history, or culture. Peru is the final stop on Leo's South American tour, which includes Argentina and Uruguay; he is expected to remain in the country until Monday, November 16.
